open_points.subject: A20 rule 6 and Required test 7
open_points.text: Another system, or a Linux or file system on which a call Registry's rules rely on — binding a listener exclusively and to IPv6 alone (A17), renaming a file into place (A17, A18) — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: Registry neither tests for it nor defines what it does there.
open_points.question: On a host whose kernel is not Linux's, must installation fail with no instance starting as Required test 7 says, or is Registry's behaviour untested and undefined because that host is “another system”?
options: Installation must detect every non-Linux kernel, fail, and start no instance.
Non-Linux installation is outside the defined behaviour and may fail, succeed, or start an instance.
open_points.default_guess: Required test 7 takes precedence: installation must fail and no instance may start.

witness.initial: The release and all of its listed dependencies are available on a host whose kernel is FreeBSD's.
events: The owner invokes the release installation on that host.
The installer determines, or does not determine, which kernel is running.
outcomes: Required test 7 requires installation to fail and no instance to start.
Rule 6's final sentence leaves behaviour on this other system undefined, so a careful installer may perform no kernel gate and allow the instance to start.
witness.observer: The owner installing and attempting to reach Registry.

open_points.subject: A20 rule 6 support boundary after removal of opening-without-following semantics
open_points.text: Another system, or a Linux or file system on which a call Registry's rules rely on — binding a listener exclusively and to IPv6 alone (A17), renaming a file into place (A17, A18) — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: Registry neither tests for it nor defines what it does there.
open_points.question: Is the displayed list exhaustive, so opening a file without following a link is no longer a host semantic on which Registry may rely and the files_artifacts guarantees must hold without it, or is that semantic still an implicit reason to declare a Linux or file system unsupported?
options: The list is exhaustive; implementations must preserve the files_artifacts guarantees without relying on Linux no-follow opening semantics.
The list is illustrative; a system that does not provide the formerly named no-follow opening semantics remains unsupported.
Registry no longer gives the safety guarantee that previously depended on opening without following a link.
open_points.default_guess: Treat the list as exhaustive and require the existing files_artifacts guarantees to hold without relying on the removed semantic.

witness.initial: Registry runs on Linux with a file-system implementation on which a requested no-follow open can resolve a pre-existing symbolic link.
events: A Registry-managed path is a symbolic link to a different file.
Registry performs an A16 or A18 file operation that previously relied on opening without following the link.
outcomes: Treating the changed list as exhaustive requires Registry to refuse or otherwise avoid accessing the link target while preserving the files_artifacts guarantee.
Treating the list as illustrative permits the implementation to rely on no-follow opening and classify this file system as unsupported after the operation follows or refuses the link.
witness.observer: The owner, who sees either protected handling of the path or access to/refusal caused by the link target.

open_points.subject: A20 release manifest identity for the Python runtime
open_points.text: A release names every dependency it runs with, at an exact version, with its digest: every Python package, direct or transitive, by the digest of its distribution file; the Python version; and the base image of VM Platform's Registry environment by its digest, which fixes the system libraries and the store's engine.
open_points.question: What concrete artifact does the Python version's required digest identify, so installation can compare it and Required test 1 can vary it?
options: Digest a separately distributed CPython runtime artifact.
Use the base-image digest as the Python runtime's digest because the interpreter is supplied by that image.
Digest the installed interpreter binary or runtime tree.
open_points.default_guess: Use a separately identified CPython runtime artifact if one exists; otherwise explicitly make the base-image digest the Python runtime's provenance rather than inventing an installed-tree digest.
consequences: A separate runtime artifact gives Python an independently verifiable identity but requires the deployment to install or expose that artifact.
Reusing the base-image digest makes Python inseparable from the image and makes the Python-digest case of Required test 1 duplicate the image check.
Digesting an installed binary or tree requires a canonical scope and can vary with packaging or installation details.
open_points.requirement: A release names every dependency it runs with, at an exact version, with its digest: every Python package, direct or transitive, by the digest of its distribution file; the Python version; and the base image of VM Platform's Registry environment by its digest, which fixes the system libraries and the store's engine.
